'''Nan Phinney''' (born 1945) is a retired American [[Accelerator Physicist|accelerator physicist]] at [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]]. She was program coordinator for the Stanford Linear Collider (SLC), the world's first [[Linear particle accelerator|linear collider]]. Her research interests are high energy colliders and linear colliders. She became an [[American Physical Society Fellows|American Physical Society Fellow]] in 1993. Her last job title at SLAC was distinguished staff scientist.

== Early life and education ==
Born in Chicago in 1945, Nan Phinney is the daughter of Thomas Ward Phinney, who trained as an electrical engineer, and Martha Louise (née Lawrence) Phinney.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|date=2008-02-17|title=Obituary for Louise Lawrence Phinney, 1922-2008 (Aged 85)|pages=4–8|work=Chicago Tribune|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/77697585/obituary-for-louise-lawrence-phinney/|access-date=2021-05-14}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> She is a granddaughter of photographer [[George R. Lawrence]].<ref name=":1" />

The family lived on the north side of Chicago, where she attended Catholic grammar school and Catholic girls' high school.<ref name=":3" />

Phinney completed a [[Bachelor of Science]] in physics and astronomy in 1966 at [[Michigan State University]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Nan Phinney|url=https://inspirehep.net/authors/993477|access-date=2021-04-12|website=inspirehep.net}}</ref> She earned an M.S. in 1968, and a Ph.D. in 1972, both degrees in [[Particle physics|high-energy physics]] at the [[Stony Brook University|State University of New York, Stony Brook]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Nan Phinney|url=https://portal.slac.stanford.edu/sites/ard_public/people/naph/Pages/default.aspx|access-date=2021-06-06|website=portal.slac.stanford.edu}}</ref> Her  dissertation was ''Trident Production in Coulomb Field,'' advised by John (Jack) Smith.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=Zierler|first=David|date=July 16, 2020|title=Interview with Nan Phinney|url=https://www.slac.stanford.edu/history/oralhistory/Phinney_Zierler_2020.pdf|access-date=April 12, 2021|website=slac.stanford.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The year 1972|url=http://www.physics.sunysb.edu/Physics/about/PAhist/1972.htm|access-date=2021-05-14|website=www.physics.sunysb.edu}}</ref>

== Career ==

=== Postdoctoral positions ===
From 1972 through 1980, Phinney held post-doc positions from [[École polytechnique|École Polytechnique]] and the [[University of Oxford]], working at [[CERN]] on high-energy particle physics experiments.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Palmer |first=Barbara |date=December 2, 2003 |title=Nan Phinney selected as Marsh O'Neill Award recipient |url=https://news.stanford.edu/news/2003/december3/marshphinney-123.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150409032926/https://news.stanford.edu/news/2003/december3/marshphinney-123.html |archive-date=April 9, 2015 |access-date=2021-04-11 |website=news.stanford.edu}}</ref> Initially she worked on the [[hyperon]] experiment on the [[Proton Synchrotron]],<ref name=":3" /> but for most of her time at CERN she worked with the CERN, Columbia, Oxford, Rockefeller group in IR-1 of the [[Intersecting Storage Rings]]. The group studied wide-angle scattering, and Phinney's work was primarily [[data acquisition]].<ref name=":3" />

=== Stanford Linear Accelerator Center ===
{{Quote box
| quote = "I thought [the linear collider] was really bold and imaginative and exciting. Anyone could build a storage ring, but this was going to be ''fun''."
| source = — Nan Phinney<ref name=":2" />
| align = right
| width = 30%
| qalign = left
| salign = right
}}
In 1981 Phinney was one of the first physicists hired to work on the [[Stanford Linear Collider]] (SLC), the world's first linear collider.<ref name=":2" /> With technical expertise and leadership qualities, she became SLC program coordinator from 1990 to 1998. She led the effort "to make the accelerator perform — an enormous challenge that took constant effort", according to [[Burton Richter|Burt Richter.]]<ref name=":2" /> Prof. David Burke said she "became an international spokesperson for the new technology as a result of her scientific expertise as well as her ability to talk to audiences ranging from scientists to government officials".<ref name=":2" />

In 2004 Phinney was elected chair of the Division of the Physics of Beams executive committee of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite news|date=May 2004|title=Election Results for 2003 DPB Executive Committee|work=Division of Physics of Beams Newsletter|url=https://higherlogicdownload.s3.amazonaws.com/APS/9cf62627-7088-4bd3-bf97-6adfc913f623/UploadedImages/Documents/may04.pdf|access-date=June 5, 2021}}</ref> She has served on the second [[International Linear Collider]] Technical Review Committee as well as the U.S. Linear Collider Steering Group Accelerator Task Force and the United Kingdom Linear Collider Machine Advisory Committee.<ref name=":2" /> According to Richter, she has brought "her hard-won wisdom and experience on linear colliders to the worldwide linear collider design efforts".<ref name=":2" />

== Awards and honors ==

* 1993 [[American Physical Society Fellows|American Physical Society Fellow]], cited "For her many contributions to the successful development and operation of the Stanford Linear Collider"<ref>{{Cite web|date=1993|title=APS Fellowship|url=http://auth.aps.commonspotcloud.com/units/dpb/fellowship/index.cfm?year=1993|access-date=2021-04-11|website=auth.aps.commonspotcloud.com|language=en}}</ref>
* 2003 Marsh O’Neill Award recipient, acknowledged for her "leadership qualities and technical ability" as program coordinator for the Stanford Linear Collider<ref name=":2" />
